Hi all, just wanted to share a 5-minute lightning talk I gave today at Wikipedia Day 2026 in Brooklyn, New York for the 25th anniversary of Wikipedia. A video of my talk can be found here, and a livestream of the entire Wikipedia Day can be found here.

The talk is titled "4 Reasons You Should Care About Math Formalization," and discusses how Wikipedia editors can use Mathlib to improve the state of WikiProject Mathematics. It was heavily influenced by @Kevin Buzzard's talk "Where is Mathematics Going?" from last year. I think that our goals and principles in the Mathlib community are greatly aligned with those of the Wikipedia community. There is much to gain from collaboration between us—If anybody here is a Wikipedia editor, or interesting in getting involved, please feel free to reach out!

Nice talk. I honestly don't know what I believe personally at this point about who should care about math formalization who isn't a mathematician -- but it's certainly "more people" and nice to see talks like yours in more venues. Hope the day was fun overall.

It was a very fun day! I agree, non-mathematicians still will not care about formalization. But many of the people using/editing Math Wikipedia are (amateur) mathematicians themselves. I feel that Wikipedia maintenance is a really difficult problem, but if we build the right technology it could also be a very fruitful, practical application of formalization.

Yeah your wikipedia <-> Mathlib database is interesting. I suppose I'm surprised someone hasn't started trying to do that already (or maybe someone indeed has!) even if it lives external to Wikipedia.
The 1000 theorems list is partially that

Ah -- right, I forgot about that. I know you said partially, I guess I don't know how to use Wikidata from an end-user perspective -- the direction that seems interesting to me is being on a Wikipedia page about the Rational Root Theorem and being able to immediately jump to Mathlib's statement of it. I see the data for doing this must be present (by hopping from https://leanprover-community.github.io/1000.html to its linked https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q180345 and seeing the Wikipedia article for english is linked there) but it'd be great if that was even easier to do from the article itself.
(Which is the point I understood Jack to be making in the talk)

Yes, it would definitely be nice if they were more tightly linked. Especially going the opposite direction—i.e. from the Wikipedia article straight to a formal implementation, would make it easier to find relevant files if you can't find them on Loogle. The main obstacle is that Wikipedia generally does not like primary research, and prefers secondary sources where possible—so an article about Mathlib would be preferred to a direct link to mathlib itself. However, there are plenty of exceptions to this rule, and I think Math Wikipedia is already so divorced from general Wikipedia (they even have their own style guide) that they may be open to accepting Mathlib as a reliable source. I have begun to add links to articles like the Structure Theorem for PIDs about Mathlib implementations, and so far have not been removed. I may add similar links to more articles and see how they are received by the WikiProject Mathematics community.

We've been trying to do something similar in formal-conjectures - among other things, we have formal statements for a quite a few conjectures that are listed on Wikipedia, with pointers to the corresponding wiki pages.

I'm not sure how valuable it is to have Wikipedia point to formalizations of results. Not too long ago I deleted an entire section of an article talking about an Isabelle formalization of ordered rings, containing such riveting results such like "the additive group is an ordered group" and "0 ≤ 1": https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Partially_ordered_ring&diff=next&oldid=1121878632

I think the idea of citing Mathlib in a paragraph talking about a certain mathematical result is a good one. But talking about the Mathlib formalization within the article just seems like fluff that won't be relevant to the vast majority of people who read it. (I don't think anyone was suggesting this, but just to be sure.)
I think there's a long way between referencing a theorem from the Mathlib docs and whatever this is, that I agree with deleting.

When I google with the purpose of finding the appropriate hypotheses / level of generality / statement for a theorem, I normally often end up reading the wikipedia page. Funnily enough, since I have gained an interest in formalisation, it is becoming quite common that the mathlib file or documentation pops up high in the google list and provides me with the answer I need. I wonder if fleshing up the Mathlib doc could make it into a bit of a math wikipedia in that sense (even usable for the non-Lean user).

@Violeta Hernández Yes, I think the example you gave of ordered rings is a good example of how this sort of thing can go wrong. Adding references to formalization is unnecessary for such basic results. I'm moreso talking about deep mathematical results with complicated proofs, where adding a small note about formalization could be helpful. (Just a single line with a reference to the proof, not a full description of the implementation.)

@Paul Lezeau Do you have a website anywhere that keeps track of the formal conjectures in the Google Deepmind repository? I am trying to avoid citing github repositories directly, since they do not really meet the typical requirements of a wikipedia source. But if there is a website that tracks the conjectures (ideally hosted under a reputable domain name, like Google.com or a .edu) then we could link to it on the Wikipedia page of the conjectures.
#Formal conjectures > New Website

#39909 adds references from Mathlib theorems to Wikidata using a new @[wikidata Q...] attribute!
Maybe people here would like to help add more?

@Snir Broshi I am working on a project right now to annotate 30,000 WikiProject Mathematics articles based on what have been formalized in Mathlib. I plan to make an announcement in a few days when I get the website up :eyes:

@Jack McCarthy That's amazing!
If you have some sort of structured data as part of your project, I would love to coordinate how we can build a Wikidata <-> Mathlib dictionary, for example using @[wikidata].

@Johan Commelin Well, there are essentially two layers of data here, depending on how much detail you want:

  1. Wikidata is article-level metadata. For the Wikipedia <--> Mathlib directory, this is most useful when the primary topic of an article corresponds a single Lean declaration. For example the Structure Theorem for PIDs Wikipedia article is "obviously" related to the Mathlib declaration docs#Module.equiv_free_prod_directSum. Right now, I am tracking this with a custom json data format, but there has been a lot of precedent for adding new Wikidata property tags to connect with public databases (e.g. for nlab they have https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Property:P4215) so it is quite possible we could get one soon for Mathlib.

  2. Wikitext is the content of the articles, and I'd argue this is where the majority of the useful/interesting math is on Wikipedia. Most Wikipedia articles are things like General Topology or Multiplication or Hilbert's Problems or Quantum Field Theory. These articles often have dozens of definitions / theorems /examples in them, but could never be pinned down to single Lean declaration. So I'm using a W3C Web Annotation Data Model format to pick out specific parts of the text and link them to Mathlib.
For (1), I think @[wikidata] can provide the inverse dictionary.
I'm curious to hear whether people think the comments in https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/39909/changes make review easier. And/or how it could be improved.

Wikidata identifiers are also used for the 1000-plus list. So it would be good if there is some logic to ensure that @[wikidata] and 1000.yaml stay in sync for everything included in 1000.yaml. (Even better if this helps identify things missing from 1000-plus so https://github.com/1000-plus/1000-plus.github.io/issues/32 and https://github.com/1000-plus/1000-plus.github.io/issues/20 can start being addressed.)

I just made a talk post in Wikiproject Mathematics for adding new "Mathlib delcaration" property to Wikidata. Those of you who have Wikidata accounts, feel free to join the discussion here.

After collecting feedback from the wikipedians, I plan to make a formal property proposal.

Joseph Myers said:

Wikidata identifiers are also used for the 1000-plus list. So it would be good if there is some logic to ensure that @[wikidata] and 1000.yaml stay in sync for everything included in 1000.yaml. (Even better if this helps identify things missing from 1000-plus so https://github.com/1000-plus/1000-plus.github.io/issues/32 and https://github.com/1000-plus/1000-plus.github.io/issues/20 can start being addressed.)

One small proposal I’d like to make here is that eventually the wikidata identifiers become the “backend” for 1000.yaml, overview.yaml, etc., and a CI step is responsible for validating/populating/updating the corresponding Mathlib declaration names in all of those files. That is, the wikidata ids become the source of truth in those files, not the decl names.

Other questions about linking to Wikidata:

  • Is use of @[wikidata] OK for both data definitions and theorems?
  • Where we have existing or new open PRs adding definitions or theorems that correspond to something in Wikidata, should we add @[wikidata] to those PRs (in addition to whatever is done to add it to existing definitions)?
  • Is it OK for multiple definitions or theorems to be linked to the same Wikidata ID?
  • Is it OK for a single definition or theorem to be linked to multiple Wikidata IDs, and what is the syntax for doing that if so?

Here's my thoughts,

  1. Yes, @[wikidata] should be used for definitions as well as theorems. Example: Q713084 <-----> docs#IsArtinianRing

  2. I don't think it should be necessary for new PRs to always add @[wikidata] tags, since that adds review time to every new feature. My preference would be to have the tags semi-autonomously maintained by a tool.

  3. For the sake of having a clean Wikidata<-->Mathlib directory, it would be nice to have a 1-to-1 bijection. Most wikidata properties only have one link (e.g. Mathworld ID, nLab, etc.) so the Mathlib property will likely be the same way: only one link to one documentation page. Although that obviously raises some issues, for example should Q196822 be linked to docs#riemannZeta or to docs#completedRiemannZeta? Perhaps in cases like this, it might be best to tag the whole page with @[wikidata]--as in put @[wikidata] in the header of Mathlib.NumberTheory.LSeries.RiemannZeta to capture the whole page?

  4. I'm not sure about going the other direction: one declaration having multiple wikidata IDs? Although my intuition is that this should be quite rare. Do you know of any examples where this would happen?
I think it is ok to link several decls to the same wikidata identifier. Eg we already have two Cauchy-Schwarz statements in Mathlib with the same wikidata attribute, right now.

1. Not necessary, but is it useful, given that the person adding a new definition or theorem has probably thought the most about what informal definitions of theorems it most closely corresponds to and so can probably assign Wikidata links more accurately than an automated process?
  2. It's an extremely common case in formalization for multiple formal statements or definitions to be needed for what informally would be thought of as "the same" result (or even if thought of as multiple results, would still only have one Wikidata entry). Sometimes informal mathematics explicitly acknowledges that there are multiple theorems but still considers them as one concept, e.g. Sylow theorems.
  3. For example, docs#Affine.Simplex.insphere clearly corresponds to both inscribed circle and inscribed sphere since mathlib doesn't have separate definitions for circles, which are just the two-dimensional version of spheres. (And those Wikidata entries would themselves correspond to multiple mathlib definitions once we have more about polygons and polyhedra and can talk about them sometimes having inscribed spheres rather than just the case for simplices.)

Inscribed circle/sphere example is great, thank you.
In this case, it seems that the mapping should not be 1-to-1. We should instead maximize flexibility by allowing multiple wikidata per mathlib decl, and conversely allowing multiple decls per wikidata.

Quick Updates

  1. Following unanimous support from WikiProject mathematics, I have now opened a property proposal to add "Mathlib Declaration ID" as a Wikidata property. This will take about a week to be approved, allowing time for community discussion.

  2. I opened PR #40440 to add 25 more Wikidata attributes to Mathlib, copying the template of Johan's #40004. Comments were added via Johan's Script (Thanks @Snir Broshi for telling me about this!). I'd love to hear suggestions about how we can build faster (possibly automated?) maintenance of cross-refs since the task ahead is quite daunting.

Jack McCarthy said:

I'd love to hear suggestions about how we can build faster (possibly automated?) maintenance of cross-refs since the task ahead is quite daunting.

I think an announcement post about @[wikidata] in #mathlib4 or #General announcements asking people to tag stuff in mathlib would be great and would cause a wave of tagging PRs! (possibly after converting the script into an automated bot workflow, and maybe adding a counter in stats)

As for the reverse mapping I think an announcement post might also help, though it'll probably be harder to cause a wave of contributions since it's at wikidata and not in mathlib.

Jack McCarthy said:

  • Following unanimous support from WikiProject mathematics, I have now opened a property proposal to add "Mathlib Declaration ID" as a Wikidata property.

Note, I notice for the property proposal that "Lean declaration" is an alias. But some mathematical concepts are not defined in Mathlib per se: if they are basic enough they might be defined in core, or if niche enough, possibly downstream in a satellite repo, but in a way that's "accepted" by the lean community in some as-yet-undefined way. (Possible example: declarations in the combinatorial games repo.) But I don't know anything about wikidata properties, so just bringing this up in case it's worth considering the edges here. :)

Yes, and 1000.yml has a few entries from downstream repos that could also use this attribute. For instance, I just opened cslib#626 to tag our variants of Church-Rosser in CSLib that we'd previously included in 1000.yaml.

I don't think wikidata should link to random repos like 1000.yml does, repos should be maintained and accept the responsibility of fixing broken links. Limiting to trusted community repos sounds good.

I don't know enough about wikidata to comment on that, I just meant it's nice that downstream repos can use this feature to tag declarations. Anyone else is then free to decide which repos they want to collect this data from.
It would be nice I suppose if this all comes together such that 1000.yaml is completely derived from usage of the wikidata attribute instead of needing a file at all, right?

@Jack McCarthy Fantastic! I left one comment on #40440. But I think this can be merged soon.

Incidentally, @Filippo A. E. Nuccio and I had a call with people from ZBMath. And they are also very interested in having this wikidata <-> mathlib dictionary. They sent us a list of 1000 most-linked concepts (together with wikidata QIDs). I'm happy to share it via DM.

What I want to build soon is a json that gives easy access to the QID <-> lean-decl dictionary. And then host that json in a stable location, and update it with CI on a regular basis.
I have translated the relevant fields of your Wikipedia proposal to French

Snir Broshi said:

As for the reverse mapping I think an announcement post might also help, though it'll probably be harder to cause a wave of contributions since it's at wikidata and not in mathlib.

I think it may be possible to automatically add the reverse direction using existing tags from Mathlib. In the proposal, I suggest the idea of using QuickStatements to add them automatically--although I will need to do a bit of testing to see if this really gives the correct mapping that we want.

Thomas Murrills said:

But some mathematical concepts are not defined in Mathlib per se: if they are basic enough they might be defined in core, or if niche enough, possibly downstream in a satellite repo, but in a way that's "accepted" by the lean community in some as-yet-undefined way.

I agree it may be good to add more Wikidata properties for Core/Batteries to cover the most basic concepts. Also expanding to other "trusted" repos like CSLib would be good. I decided to scope the proposal to only Mathlib because that is what fits most cleanly into the existing Wikidata format--a single project with a single documentation page url. It's worth noting that there was a separate proposal immediately after mine to add a generic "formal proof" property, but it was quite quickly rejected/withdrawn.

https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/compare/master...jcommelin:mathlib4:wikidata-json is my proposed patch for generating a json file with the cross ref dictionary.

I've tested it, and you can see the result it produces here: https://github.com/jcommelin/crossref-exports/blob/master/crossrefs.json

Before merging that we probably want to change from using a PAT (presumably what you have stored in secrets.CROSSREFS_PUSH_TOKEN to a GitHub app installed under leanprover-community. Claude will probably be able to walk you through it, or I can help too.
Also happy to review the lean part of that patch if there’s a PR :)
@Jack McCarthy do I understand correctly that you already have a lot more candidates that can be turned into PRs just like #40440?

Yes, see https://wikilean.jackmccarthy.org/ -- I am building a database
But obvious disclaimer is that they are all AI-generated

Before merging that we probably want to change from using a PAT (presumably what you have stored in secrets.CROSSREFS_PUSH_TOKEN to a GitHub app installed under leanprover-community. Claude will probably be able to walk you through it, or I can help too.

I would love to get some help. Would you mind taking on that part of the process?

But obvious disclaimer is that they are all AI-generated

Wow, that's pretty cool!
Yes, am quite excited about it, but is still a WIP with many missing features. Proper announcement coming soon.

I've now created

feat(scripts): export wikidata/stacks/kerodon cross-references as JSON #40701

with the patch that I linked to above.

"Mathlib Declaration ID" is now officially a property on Wikidata
https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Property:P14534
Congratulations!
